newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRENCH ELECTIONS - SUMMARY OF MAIN ISSUES.
newsitem.headline: FRENCH ELECTIONS - SUMMARY OF MAIN ISSUES.

text.p: Following is a summary of the main issues behind France's two-stage parliamentary election on May 25 and June 1:
WHY EARLY ELECTIONS?

French President Jacques Chirac said he wanted an early vote to allow French people a say on the speed and scale of economic reform and put France in a strong position in negotiations on Europe ahead on the launch of a single currency

Other explanations: making it easier to continue austerity drive, winning Chirac a "friendly" parliament until end of term in 2002, limiting potential damage from judicial inquiries into party financing by allowing Chirac to drop some ministers
CHANCES OF PULLING IT OFF?
Opinion polls consistently show RPR/UDF winning majority of seats in the 577-seat National Assembly but with majority cut.
Polls cover predictions for 555 metropolitan France seats, show Socialists gaining some ground and importantly that about a third of voters are undecided or could change their minds.

Analysts question reliability of polls, and say vote could be close. Socialists could benefit from unpopularity of Prime Minister Alain Juppe, bad record on unemployment, and chance of National Front vote going to the Left in the second round
HOW ARE MARKETS REACTING?

-- franc, government debt and shares holding up relatively well on assumption centre-right will keep power but vulnerable to uncertainty and any sign of Socialist catch-up. However, some say differences in Left/Right manifestos not too dramatic

-- PIBOR interest rate futures, where foreign investors most active, have recovered from initial fall but still vulnerable. Bank of France seen well placed to defend currency if needed with healthy reserves, unlikely to hike official interest rates.
-- stock market intermittently affected by opinion polls but seen less vulnerable than debt to Socialist ascendancy to extent some say Socialists could help consumption.
WHAT DOES IT MEAN FOR EUROPEAN MONETARY UNION?
-- centre-right committed to launch of euro single currency.
-- Socialist stance summed up as "Yes, But"; oppose dogmatic application of Maastricht treaty criteria; playing safe due risk of alienating potential Communist party partner, which anti-EMU.

-- Socialists have set four conditions for joining euro: 1) entry of Italy, Spain from start and Britain too if it wants. 2) creation of an "economic government" as political counterwieght to European Central Bank. 3) creation of solidarity and growth pact to boost jobs 4) policies to ensure euro is not overvalued.
-- they also want to review the EU "stability pact" designed to keep budget deficits down after launch of euro.
WHAT DOES IT MEAN FOR FRENCH ECONOMIC POLICIES?
-- centre-right coalition seen sticking largely to current policy, perhaps with more "liberal" touch on curbing state role.

-- committed to euro single currency, curbing state spending to keep rises below inflation, continuing programme of income tax cuts, aims to lower labour costs by easing social charges, mainly for small and medium sized businesses.

-- further austerity expected in 1998 budget under RPR/UDF, while Socialist party questioning belt-tightening, seeking to promote employment and economic growth at same time by creating 700,000 jobs with state support and reducing work week to 35 from 39 hours without cutting pay to increase purchasing power
-- room for manoeuvre for any government limited: both sides show general acceptance of need to prevent further rise in state deficit to head of risk of big debt repayments in future.
-- ruling RPR/UDF coalition says its public spending cuts and tax reductions will boost business confidence, leave way clear for low interest rates, pave the way for more investment, growth and jobs
-- position still unclear on more "free-market" politicians, like former finance minister Alain Madelin, who may be brought into a new right-wing government
-- partial privatisation of France Telecom, due in May, has been delayed by four weeks.
-- Socialist and Communist parties wary of of privatisation, notably France Telecom, defence group Thomson-CSF and Air France but Socialists may be open to sales of minority stakes
